Primer 1 left you with vectors. Stand several equal-length vectors side by side
and you have the rectangle you will actually analyse: one row per observation —
a student, a patient, a session — and one column per variable. In the
tidyverse that rectangle is a **tibble**. For the full explanation, see
[the R primer](r-primer.qmd).

## Building a tibble

`tibble()` takes named vectors and lines them up as columns. Each one must be
the same length.

```{webr}
library(tibble)

students <- tibble(
  student_id = c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04"),
  batch      = c("2023", "2023", "2024", "2024"),
  attendance = c(88, 72, 95, 64),
  passed     = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

students
```

Read the header it prints. `# A tibble: 4 × 4` is four rows by four columns,
and under each column name sits its type: `<chr>` for text, `<dbl>` for a
number with decimals, `<lgl>` for `TRUE`/`FALSE`. A plain `data.frame` tells
you none of that until you ask.

Note that `batch` is `<chr>`, not a number. Years used as labels are text —
you would never take their mean.

## Looking at one

Four questions cover almost everything you will want to know about a table you
have just been handed.

```{webr}
nrow(students)
ncol(students)
names(students)
glimpse(students)
```

`glimpse()` is the function you will reach for when something goes wrong. It
turns the table on its side so every column gets one line — name, type, first
few values — however wide the data. Nine times out of ten the problem is that a
column is text when you thought it was a number, and `glimpse()` shows you
that in one look: `$ attendance <dbl>` is a number you can average,
`$ attendance <chr>` is not.

## Pulling out a column

`$` takes one column out of the rectangle and hands it back as a plain vector —
exactly the kind of thing Primer 1 taught you to work with.

```{webr}
students$attendance
mean(students$attendance)
```

That is the whole pattern: a tibble is a bundle of vectors, and `$` unwraps
one.

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: build a tibble"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Three viva stations were marked out of 10: History scored 8, Exam scored 7 and
Counselling scored 9. Put them into a tibble called `viva` with two columns,
`station` and `marks`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tibble
viva <- tibble(
  station = ______,
  marks   = ______
)

viva
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tibble
#| solution: true
viva <- tibble(
  station = c("History", "Exam", "Counselling"),
  marks   = c(8, 7, 9)
)

viva
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tibble
#| check: true
expected <- tibble::tibble(
  station = c("History", "Exam", "Counselling"),
  marks   = c(8, 7, 9)
)
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(.result), as.data.frame(expected)))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — three rows, two columns.")
} else if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is not a table yet. Use tibble() with two named columns.")
} else if (ncol(.result) != 2) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You need exactly two columns: station and marks.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Check the spelling and order of the station names.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_tibble"}
Each column is a vector, so each one needs its own `c()`. The station names are
text and go in quotation marks; the marks are numbers and do not.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: average the attendance"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Using the `students` tibble from the top of the page, work out the mean
attendance across the four students. Pull the column out with `$`, then take
its mean.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mean
students <- tibble(
  student_id = c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04"),
  batch      = c("2023", "2023", "2024", "2024"),
  attendance = c(88, 72, 95, 64),
  passed     = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mean
#| solution: true
students <- tibble(
  student_id = c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04"),
  batch      = c("2023", "2023", "2024", "2024"),
  attendance = c(88, 72, 95, 64),
  passed     = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

mean(students$attendance)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mean
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 79.75))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — mean attendance is 79.75%.")
} else if (!is.numeric(.result) || length(.result) != 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the column itself, not its average. Wrap it in mean().")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 319))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the total of the four values. mean() divides it by four.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Take the column with students$attendance, then pass it to mean().")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mean"}
`students$attendance` gives you a vector of four numbers. `mean()` takes it
from there.
:::
:::
